title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 17: People v. Genosa: The Battered Woman Syndrome
keywords: Article 13 of the Revised Penal Code
Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act of 2004
primary_topics: Chapter 17 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's account of People v. Genosa, the first Philippine case to examine the viability of the battered woman syndrome as a defense in a prosecution for parricide, a Decision he wrote only after immersing himself in medical and scientific study of the phenomenon.

His exposition of the syndrome itself -- the definition of a battered woman, the common personality traits, and the three-phase cycle of violence of tension-building, acute battering and tranquil reconciliation, together with the illusion of absolute interdependency that keeps the woman in the relationship.

The Court's ruling: that the defense proved only one full cycle rather than the required two, that unlawful aggression had ceased when Ben went to bed, and that self-defense therefore failed -- while two mitigating circumstances, diminished will power and passion and obfuscation, and the absence of treachery, reduced the death sentence.

The aftermath: Justice Ynares-Santiago's dissent for complete self-defense and acquittal, the 10-4 vote, and the Postscript on Republic Act No. 9262, which took effect on March 27, 2004 and exculpates victim-survivors of the syndrome even absent the elements of self-defense.
sub_topics: He explains why the case takes center stage in an age of advocacy for women's rights, and that writing the Decision required an in-depth medical and scientific study of the syndrome and of how foreign jurisdictions had applied it.

The facts: Marivic Genosa was abused by her husband for over eight of their twelve years of marriage, and on the evening of November 15, 1995, while she was eight months pregnant, another violent incident ended in Ben Genosa's death; admitting the killing, she anchored her prayer for acquittal on the novel theory of the battered woman syndrome.
The issues after her 1997 arraignment and conviction for parricide: whether she acted in self-defense and in defense of her fetus, and whether treachery attended the killing.

The definition of a battered woman -- one repeatedly subjected to forceful physical or psychological behavior by a man to coerce her without concern for her rights -- and the requirement that the couple pass through the battering cycle at least twice.

The common personality traits: low self-esteem, traditional beliefs about home, family and the female sex role, emotional dependence on the dominant male, a tendency to accept responsibility for the batterer's actions, and false hopes of improvement.

The tension-building phase, in which minor battering occurs and the woman placates the batterer, her passive behavior legitimizing his belief that he may abuse her, until the violence spirals out of control.

The acute battering incident, marked by brutality and destructiveness, during which she has no control, feels detached from the pain, and knows from experience that resistance would only worsen her condition.

The tranquil phase of remorseful reconciliation, in which the batterer begs forgiveness and promises to change and she convinces herself that this good, gentle and caring man is the real person she loves -- the phase in which she is most thoroughly tormented psychologically.

The illusion of absolute interdependency: each partner emotionally dependent on the other, each perhaps believing it better to die than to be separated, so that her state of mind metamorphoses and cannot be judged from the viewpoint of an ordinary reasonable person.

The expert testimony: Lenore Walker on how the cyclical violence immobilizes the woman's ability to act in her own interests and on the greater danger at the point of separation; Dr. Natividad Dayan on poverty, self-blame and the duty to keep the family intact; and Dr. Alfredo Pajarillo on posttraumatic stress disorder and learned helplessness.

The Court's finding that the defense fell short: Marivic described the tension-building phase of the fatal incident in adequate detail, but a single episode did not prove the syndrome, since the couple must have gone through the cycle at least twice, and the experts testified theoretically without presenting the factual experiences on which they based their conclusion.

Self-defense analysis: the existence of the syndrome does not by itself establish a right to kill; unlawful aggression is the most essential element, and here a sufficient interval had passed, Marivic having withdrawn to the children's bedroom while Ben ceased his attack and went to bed.

The Court's important qualification: had Ben still been awaiting her, the imminence of the threat would not have ceased, and where the brutalized person already suffers from the syndrome, further evidence of actual physical assault at the time of the killing is not required, since to make her await an obvious deadly attack would sentence her to murder by installments.

Mitigating circumstances: the repeated severe beatings constituted cumulative provocation that broke down her psychological resistance and self-control, and this psychological paralysis diminished her will power under paragraphs 9 and 10 of Article 13 of the Revised Penal Code.

Passion and obfuscation: Ben had threatened to kill her while dragging her by the neck toward the cabinet where he kept a gun, and she was eight months pregnant, so that the attempt was on her life and her fetus's; with Dr. Pajarillo's testimony on reliving the trauma, there was no considerable period in which she could have recovered her equanimity.

Treachery rejected: the trial court had inferred it merely from the fracture at the back of Ben's head, but the prosecution never established how and when he was attacked, a killing preceded by a quarrel forewarns the deceased, and nothing showed she deliberately chose a risk-free method -- so the death sentence was vacated and reduced to six years and one day of prision mayor to fourteen years, eight months and one day of reclusion temporal, qualifying her for parole.

The Epilogue he quotes in full: the Court agonized over applying a novel theory, took great effort beyond the normal manner of deciding, learned much with the help of the solicitor general and Atty. Katrina Legarda, and set out three conditions under which battered woman syndrome self-defense could succeed in a future case.

The dissent of Justice Consuelo Ynares-Santiago: the tension-building phase was shown more than once, the acute phase by beatings and threats with a bolo and cutter, the tranquil phase by repeated kiss-and-make-up episodes, so that Marivic was afflicted with the syndrome and entitled to complete self-defense -- joined by Chief Justice Davide and Justices Gutierrez and Martinez in voting to acquit.

The outcome and Postscript: a decisive 10-4 vote with no motion for reconsideration filed by Marivic, and Republic Act No. 9262, effective March 27, 2004, which exculpates victim-survivors of the syndrome, penalizes other acts of violence against women and children, and entitles victims to protection orders -- with its effect on the Genosa ruling left an open question.

stances.claim: The battered woman syndrome was not established in this case, because a cycle of violence requires that each phase be shown in at least two battering episodes, and the defense proved only the tension-building phase of the fatal incident.
stances.rhetorical_move: definition-then-application: he first sets out the clinical requirements of the syndrome at length, then measures the evidence against them element by element

stances.claim: The existence of the syndrome does not by itself establish a legal right to kill the abusive partner; unlawful aggression remains the most essential element of self-defense, and here it had ceased when Ben stopped his attack and went to bed.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal discipline: he separates sympathy from legal entitlement and insists the evidence still be tested in the context of self-defense

stances.claim: Where the brutalized person already suffers from the syndrome, further evidence of actual physical assault at the time of the killing is not required, since to require her to await an obvious deadly attack would amount to sentencing her to murder by installments.
stances.rhetorical_move: prospective rule-setting: having denied the defense on these facts, he states the conditions under which it would succeed, and seals them with a vivid phrase

stances.claim: The repeated beatings constituted cumulative provocation producing a psychological paralysis that diminished her will power, and the threat to her life and her unborn child's produced passion and obfuscation, so that both mitigating circumstances should be credited to her.
stances.rhetorical_move: expert-grounded mitigation: he quotes Dr. Dayan's report and Dr. Pajarillo's testimony to convert clinical findings into statutory mitigating circumstances

stances.claim: Justice Ynares-Santiago's dissent maintained that all three phases were established, that BWS with a pattern of threatening behavior takes the place of unlawful aggression, and that Marivic was entitled to complete self-defense and acquittal.
stances.rhetorical_move: full restatement of the opposing opinion, including its charge that recognizing the syndrome would be an empty victory if the Court closed its eyes to this case's antecedents

notable_anecdotes: His own immersion: he relates that to be able to write the Decision he had to immerse himself in an in-depth medical and scientific study of the syndrome and of its treatment in foreign jurisprudence.

The night of the killing: he recounts that Ben threatened to kill Marivic while dragging her by the neck toward the cabinet where he kept a gun, that she was eight months pregnant, and that she later pried open the drawer, took the weapon and shot him.
Walker's finding on separation: he cites the American psychologist's research that abuse often escalates at the point of separation, when battered women are in greater danger of dying.

The fracture at the back of the head: the trial court had inferred treachery and imposed death merely from the open, depressed, circular fracture found on Ben's body, though the prosecution never showed how or when he was attacked.

The Court agonizing: in the Epilogue he describes how the Court agonized over applying a novel theory as a modern-day reality, took effort beyond the normal manner of deciding, and credits the solicitor general and Atty. Katrina Legarda with helping it learn.

Marivic's acquiescence: he notes that she seemed to agree with the majority, since she filed no motion for reconsideration and accepted the Decision, having already served the minimum of her reduced sentence while detained.
The law that followed: he closes by reporting that after the Decision became final, Congress passed RA 9262, effective March 27, 2004, and leaves open how the new law would affect the Genosa ruling.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's account of People v. Genosa, the first Philippine case to consider the viability of the battered woman syndrome as a defense to parricide, a Decision he could write, he said, only after immersing himself in medical and scientific study of the phenomenon and its treatment abroad. Marivic Genosa had been abused by her husband for more than eight of their twelve married years when, on the evening of November 15, 1995, eight months pregnant, she killed him; admitting the killing, she claimed the syndrome as self-defense. He set out the clinical background at length: the definition of a battered woman, who must have passed through the battering cycle at least twice; the traits of low self-esteem, emotional dependence, self-blame and false hope; and the three phases of the cycle of violence -- tension-building, in which her placatory behavior legitimizes the batterer's sense of entitlement; the acute battering incident, brutal and beyond her control; and the tranquil phase of remorseful reconciliation, in which she is most thoroughly tormented. He described the illusion of absolute interdependency and drew on Lenore Walker, Dr. Natividad Dayan and Dr. Alfredo Pajarillo on immobilization, learned helplessness and posttraumatic stress. The Court nevertheless held that the defense fell short, since only one full sequence was proved and the experts testified theoretically without the factual basis for their conclusion, and that self-defense failed because unlawful aggression, its most essential element, had ceased when Ben stopped attacking and went to bed. Yet it cautioned that where a brutalized person already suffers from the syndrome, no further proof of actual assault at the moment of killing is needed, for to make her await an obvious deadly attack would sentence her to murder by installments. Crediting cumulative provocation and psychological paralysis under paragraphs 9 and 10 of Article 13, and passion and obfuscation arising from the threat to her life and her fetus's, and rejecting treachery as unproven, the Court vacated her death sentence, reduced it to prision mayor to reclusion temporal and qualified her for parole. Justice Ynares-Santiago dissented for complete self-defense and acquittal, joined by three others, making the vote 10-4, and the chapter closes with Republic Act No. 9262, effective March 27, 2004, whose effect on the ruling he left an open question.
